Senses.Explanation: Literally ‘guest within host,’ one of the four positional names built from guest and host. In the Linji-house definition preserved by The Eye of Humans and Gods, the teacher having a ‘nose-hole’ is host-within-host, the student having one is host-within-guest, the teacher lacking one is guest-within-host, and the student lacking one is guest-within-guest; the compilation immediately warns that this differs from Caodong guest-and-host. That explicit definition makes ‘guest within host’ (主中賓) here the position in which ‘the teacher lacks a nose-hole; this is named guest within host’ (師家無鼻孔，名主中賓), rather than a free synonym for the whole guest-host pair. The same compilation records the term as a question answered by Fengxue (‘the returning simurgh, the two luminaries renewed’), as a verse heading, and in several masters' complete four-position catechisms. Later records continue asking ‘what is guest within host?’ and answer with fresh lines such as ‘green mountains cover white clouds’ and ‘empty-handed, mingling with the dusty world.’ The changing answers remain answers to one named public-interview position; this entry reports them without choosing a hidden interpretation.
Senses.Note: 344 hits in the wave plan. The source compilation explicitly distinguishes Linji and Caodong formulations, so this corpus-wide sense does not silently transfer Caodong bent/upright or interchange language into it. The gloss order follows the graphs: guest within host (主中賓); compare host within guest (賓中主). One sense, because poems and catechism answers keep the same positional label.

Senses.Explanation: Host, master of a house, or the one in charge (主人), plus a personifying honorific such as 'sir' or 'master' (公), forms the personified 'master-in-charge' (主人公). The locus classicus is Ruiyan Shiyan (瑞巖師彥), who every day sat on his rock and called out to himself — 'each day he calls "Master!" and himself answers "Yes"' (每日喚主人公復應諾) — then warned himself 'stay wide awake… don't let anyone deceive you' (惺惺著…莫受人謾); this is case 12 of the Wumenguan (無門關, 'Gateless Checkpoint'). The record groups it with Linji's 'true person of no rank' (無位真人) and 'mind itself is buddha' (即心是佛): 'many take Ruiyan's master-in-charge and Linji's true person of no rank…' (多將箇瑞巖主人公臨濟無位真人). Asked 'what is Zhaozhou's master-in-charge?' (如何是趙州主人公), Zhaozhou barks (咄): 'this bucket-hooping fellow!' (這箍桶漢, a menial-cooper insult). The record sets it against the 'bright, numinous' identity-consciousness (昭昭靈靈的識神), faulting the one who guards that and imagines he has realized the master: 'guarding the bright-numinous identity-consciousness and taking that to be realizing the master-in-charge' (守住個昭昭靈靈的識神便是悟得主人公也). Zhaozhou identifies it in the first person in his own record: 'before there was a world, this nature already was; when the world perishes, this nature does not perish. Since once seeing this old monk — it is no one else, just this master-in-charge' (未有世界早有此性世界壞時此性不壞從一見老僧後更不是別人只是箇主人公), continuing 'why hunt outside for this one?' (者箇更向外覔作麼) (the Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Zhaozhou Shen 趙州諗禪師語錄, inside the Recorded Sayings of the Venerable Ancients 古尊宿語錄, C077n1710; the saying is raised again as a case in Yuanwu's Recorded Sayings 圓悟語錄, T47n1997). Deployed as a standing examination question, 'where is the master-in-charge?' appears as (主人公在甚麼處) 70 times in 44 allowlist texts and in the graph variant (主人公在什麼處) 26 times in 18 texts. It is typically framed 'no dream, no thought, no seeing, no hearing — where then is the master-in-charge?' (無夢無想無見無聞主人公在甚麼處, so B27n0152; punctuated with 'just when asleep' 正睡著時 in J25nB171); the record tells how Xueyan Qin (雪巖欽) put it to Gaofeng (高峰): 'Gaofeng strove bitterly five years; the pillow slid to the floor, and he greatly awakened' (峰苦志五年，推枕子墮地，大悟, J26nB177, also J26nB178). Another exchange answers 'where is the master-in-charge right now?' (主人公即今在什麼處) with 'no autumn wind fanning, yet the cassia scent drifts' (秋風不扇，桂蕊飄香) in three lamp records (X81n1568, X82n1571; X80n1566 writes the variant graphs 桂蕋 and 甚麼處). The Chan House Tortoise-Mirror (禪家龜鑑) lists it among the things called out: 'under the ancestral masters' gate there are also those who call "Amitābha" and those who call "Master!"' (祖師門下亦有或喚阿彌陀佛者，或喚主人公者, X63n1255). Tianru Weize gives a second explicit equivalence in his own record: 'what is called mind? Mind, on each person's own share, is called oneself and is also called the master-in-charge' (何者謂之心？心在諸人分上喚作自己，又喚作主人公). This Tianru Weize witness is independent of the Ruiyan self-calling and Zhaozhou exchanges.
Senses.Note: The central corpus use is contrastive: the recurring warning is against taking the identity-consciousness (識神), the 'bright and numinous' (昭昭靈靈), for the master-in-charge (esp. B27n0152). Origin: Ruiyan's self-calling (Wumenguan case 12). Compare 'true person of no rank' (無位真人) — the record itself lists Ruiyan's master-in-charge and Linji's true person of no rank side by side as equivalents. Current allowlist counts: master-in-charge (主人公) 738 hits in 198 texts; the graph variant 'master-in-charge' (主人翁), with 'old man' as the honorific (翁), 242 hits in 98 texts; and the calling formula 'calling the master-in-charge' (喚主人公), 54 hits in 35 texts. A second witness to the identity-consciousness contrast: 'wrongly construing the flickering shimmer-and-shadow of the bright-numinous before one's eyes, taking it for the master-in-charge' (妄自和會箇目前昭昭靈靈底浮光幻影。認為主人公, B25n0145 0796a06).

AlternateTargets: the sword that brings people to life
Senses.Explanation: (活) to bring-to-life / revive + (人) person + (劍) (a double-edged sword): 'the sword that gives life.' It runs as the standard complement of (殺人刀) ('the sword that kills'): the dominant pairing sets a life-giving (劍) against a killing (刀), though the graphs are not fixed to the verbs (活人刀 and 殺人劍 also occur — see the Note; and the entry 殺人刀). (活人劍) occurs 282× in 104 allowlist files, and the two contiguous as (殺人刀活人劍) 25× in 12 files. The pair is answered as a set — '(殺人刀)，(活人劍)，(死者死)，(活者活)' (古庭善堅's 拈) — and posed as paired test-questions with recorded answers: '(如何是殺人刀)？」(師打云)：「(一棒打殺)。」…「(如何是活人劍)？」(師打云)：「(自領出去)」' (密雲圓悟, 上堂). Masters are measured by whether they hold it: '(黃檗只有殺人刀)，(且無活人劍)' (a 妙喜 gauge raised in 天隱圓修's record). It is split by timing — '(一轉語是殺人刀)、(一轉語是活人劍)、(一轉語殺活同時)、(一轉語殺活不同時)' (殺活同時 21× in 17 files). (玉林通琇), in an (上堂) at his (師翁) (幻有大和尚)'s (誕日設供): '(最初秪見師翁殺人刀未見師翁活人劍)…(亦有殺人刀亦有活人劍)'. And in verse: '(活人須是活人劍)，(殺賊應還殺賊刀)'. The texts deploy the pair in (拈古), (上堂), and test-questions without assigning it a gloss, and neither does this entry.
Senses.Note: The complement of (殺人刀) (t_d7167b5f3236); the two entries cross-reference. This entry curates the (活人劍) pole and witnesses independent of the (殺人刀) entry's (which used T48n2003, T47n1997, J25nB171×2). The dominant graphic split is killing = (刀) (single-edged blade), life-giving = (劍) (double-edged sword), and the canonical contiguous dyad is (殺人刀活人劍) (25× in 12 files; the reversed contiguous 殺人劍活人刀 does not occur). But the graphs are not welded to the verbs: (活人刀) also occurs 28× in 23 allowlist files and (殺人劍) 11× in 9 (e.g. 殺人須有活人刀，活人須有殺人劍, J25nB174 0713c09) — a strong tendency, not a contrast the texts uniformly keep. The pair is deployed three ways here: (1) answered as a set (殺人刀，活人劍，死者死，活者活); (2) split by timing — (殺活同時) / (殺活不同時) (21× in 17 files); (3) used as a gauge measuring a master (黃檗 has only the killing sword). Roster witnesses: (密雲圓悟) (J10nA158) and (玉林通琇) (B27n0152); further witnesses (古庭善堅) (J25nB163) and the off-roster (天岸昇) (J26nB187) / (石奇通雲) (J26nB183) left unattributed. The '(黃檗只有殺人刀)' line is a raised (妙喜) quotation inside (天隱圓修)'s (語錄) (cb:mulu 舉古), hence null. The RelatedTerms beyond the dyad are attested in the same breath as it: '(須知殺中有活擒縱人天)。(活中有殺權衡佛祖)' (圓悟佛果禪師語錄, T47n1997) for (擒縱), and '(殺人刀)、(活人劍)，(赤心片片)，(踞虎頭)、(收虎尾)，(始終不移)，(把住則孤峰坐斷無人識)，(放行則亙古風光照大千)' (笑堂和尚語錄, J28nB206) for (把住)/(放行).

Senses.Explanation: The two graphs mean “living” and “phrase or utterance”: “a living phrase,” attested 412 times in 128 allowlisted texts. One direct definition is contrastive: “Speech containing speech is called a dead phrase; speech without speech is called a living phrase.” Another says that a phrase which does not fall into verbal explanation, does not drop into a track of reasoning, does not enter thought, does not permit deliberation, changes a thousand and ten thousand ways, and meets opposition on eight sides is called a living phrase. Gulin Qingmao records another description: “As for its living: a net will not hold it, a call will not turn its head, the ancient sages do not arrange it, and to this day it has no place.” A recurrent instruction says, “Investigate the living phrase; do not investigate the dead phrase.” Blue Cliff Record says that recognition under a living phrase is never forgotten, whereas recognition under a dead phrase cannot save oneself. Records also ask “What is a living phrase?” and preserve different answers, including “obtained within death.” An intermediate category, “a phrase neither dead nor living,” also occurs. These are the records' descriptions and classifications; the entry does not infer a hidden force behind them.
Senses.Note: The opposite “dead phrase” occurs 372 times. “Investigate the living phrase” occurs 90 times, and “under the living phrase” occurs 33 times. Gulin also records the explicit reversal, “A dead phrase is precisely a living phrase; a living phrase is precisely a dead phrase.” The contrast is therefore reported as a recurring textual classification rather than imposed as an invariant property of particular words.

Senses.Explanation: The first graph means “alive”; the repeated fish graph depicts lively, darting movement: “alive and darting.” The literal fish wording remains visible in a verse about fine fish beneath the frozen Yellow River: they are “alive and darting, yet cannot leap out.” Chan records apply the expression to people, sayings, movement, stillness, and “this matter.” One hall address says, “In motion, constantly still; at rest, alive and darting,” and then says that motion and stillness are both forgotten. A case comment says that this matter “rolls and turns, alive and darting, like a pearl running on a tray, without a stagnant trace.” Blue Cliff Record requires an “alive and darting fellow” whose phrases and workings accord. Other records ask directly for “the alive-and-darting phrase” or place the expression beside “clean and naked, without turning back and forth.” These are the texts’ stated predicates and comparisons; the entry does not assign them an unstated inner quality.
Senses.Note: The headword occurs 229 times in 99 allowlisted texts. The common alternate spelling using the ordinary graph for lively occurs 175 times in 82 texts; the older Linji spelling with a different fish-side graph occurs 7 times in 4 texts. The adverbial form occurs 63 times in 37 texts. One text asks directly for the “alive-and-darting phrase.” The fish, person, phrase, and appraisal deployments share one descriptive expression rather than requiring separate senses.

Senses.Explanation: (鼻) nose + (孔) hole: "the nostrils." In the corpus the word is deployed overwhelmingly as a person's handle/spot — the place by which one is taken hold of, led, possessed, or lost, and by which one holds one's own ground. Attested collocations (grep counts, allowlist): it is pierced and led like an ox — (穿卻鼻孔) / (穿鼻孔) (29), "pull the nostrils around," (拽轉鼻孔 4), e.g. "already had the nostrils pierced by the whisk" (已被拂子穿卻鼻孔) and "had his nostrils casually pulled around by that layman" (被箇俗漢等閑拽轉鼻孔); it is placed in another's control — "the nostrils are in someone else's hands," (鼻孔在別人手裏 9), (殊不知鼻孔在別人手裏); it is lost — (失卻鼻孔) (11), and asked after as a fault, "why have you lost your nostrils these days?" (你日來因甚失卻鼻孔); it is groped for and found — (摸著鼻孔) (82), (摸著舊時鼻孔)，(依前只在面皮上便見); and it is held up in independence — (鼻孔遼天) (287) / (鼻孔撩天) (208) ("nostrils to the sky"), (人人鼻孔遼天)，(各各壁立千仞). The texts draw the contrast between (鼻孔在別人手裏) (a nose held by another) and (鼻孔遼天)／(撩天) (a nose held to the sky). They also say that a speaker seeks to "breathe through the same nostrils as the old ones" (與古人同一鼻孔出氣), making the same body opening the shared outlet of a voice. The word carries no gloss in the texts beyond the body-part and its use as this handle or outlet, and neither does this entry.
Senses.Note: One corpus-wide idiom (6246 occ / 386 texts). All curated occurrences are stock deployments of the idiom, not a named master's coinage, so MasterName is null. The literal graphs mean the nostrils; the recurring collocations (穿/拽/失卻/摸著/遼天) are the attested pattern — pierced/led like an ox, held by another, lost, groped for, or held to the sky. Not to be confused with the separate compound-heads (鼻孔遼天) / (鼻孔撩天) (their own idioms).

Occurrences.Kwic: 殊不知鼻孔在別人手裏。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: (佛果圜悟禪師碧巖錄) (Yuanwu's Blue Cliff Record); prose commentary — the nostrils held in another's hands as the image of being controlled. Stock idiom, MasterName null.

Occurrences.Kwic: 已被拂子穿卻鼻孔
Occurrences.AttributionNote: (朝宗禪師語錄); the nostrils pierced by the raised whisk (拂子) — the ox-lead image applied to an interlocutor. Span crosses lb 0254b07→0254b08. Stock idiom, MasterName null.

Occurrences.Kwic: 被箇俗漢等閑拽轉鼻孔。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: (大慧普覺禪師語錄) (Dahui's record; passage in the 塔銘 section) — the nostrils pulled around (拽轉) by another. Stock idiom, MasterName null.

Occurrences.Kwic: 人人鼻孔遼天，各各壁立千仞。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: (列祖提綱錄); the contrasting pole — nostrils held to the sky (遼天), everyone standing on his own thousand-fathom wall. Stock idiom, MasterName null.

Occurrences.Kwic: 摸著舊時鼻孔，依前只在面皮上便見。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: (雪巖祖欽禪師語錄); groping for and finding one's own old nostrils (摸著舊時鼻孔). Span crosses lb 0633c05→0633c06. Stock idiom, MasterName null.

Occurrences.Kwic: 你日來因甚失卻鼻孔？
Occurrences.AttributionNote: (雨山和尚語錄); a master's test-question treating loss of the nostrils (失卻鼻孔) as a fault, answered "pierced yours, master" (穿卻和尚的). Stock idiom, MasterName null.

Occurrences.Kwic: 師曰我鼻孔被大師𢬟得痛不徹
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Old Venerables Record; an attendant says, 'My nostrils were pinched by the great master so painfully it has not gone through.' This is the literal physical body-part anchor against which the corpus's handle idioms were re-tested.

Occurrences.Kwic: 山僧如此批判，要與古人同一鼻孔出氣。且道諸人還甘麼？
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Xingkong Zhen's record; 'this mountain monk judges it this way in order to breathe through the same nostrils as the old ones.' The shared-breath idiom extends the same bodily image to speaking in concert.
